standard.title: Evaluating respectful relationships
standard.description: evaluate the influence of respect, empathy, power and coercion on establishing and maintaining respectful relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain and apply skills to communicate assertively when seeking, giving or denying consent (AC9HP8P07). They have previously examined roles of respect, empathy, power and coercion in respectful relationships (AC9HP8P04). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to evaluation — assessing how these factors operate and what happens when the balance shifts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate how respect, empathy, power and coercion influence whether relationships are established and maintained as respectful, including the influence of historical inequity and the forms violence can take.

nodes.label: Power and coercion in relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how power imbalances and coercion undermine respectful relationships
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a power imbalance in a relationship scenario and evaluate how it affects the ability of both parties to maintain respect and autonomy
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how the balance of power influences the nature of relationships; evaluate the characteristics of positive, respectful relationships against the rights and ethical responsibilities of individuals; propose actions when a relationship is not respectful
wider: Investigate how historical patterns of inequity, violence and discrimination have lasting intergenerational effects on wellbeing — evaluate strategies for building cultural awareness and empathy that contribute to reconciliation

Analyse how bullying, racism and gender-based violence take different forms (verbal, physical, emotional, sexual, economic) in face-to-face and online environments — evaluate which forms are most commonly underrecognised and why
Investigate how demonstrating support for truth-telling causes can build cultural awareness, empathy and more respectful relationships at community level
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate how power imbalances operate cannot assess the role of respect and empathy as countervailing forces in Node 2 — the constructive analysis requires first having established where and how coercion undermines relationships.

response_modes.reason: Students often name that power imbalances are harmful without evaluating how they operate — the mechanism by which coercion undermines respect and autonomy. The structured reasoning investment is in building the evaluative chain: what power imbalance, in what relationship context, what effect on each party's rights, what does a respectful response look like. The intergenerational inequity direction requires this same chain applied at a historical and cultural scale.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The intergenerational inequity direction and the forms-of-violence analysis each require applying the evaluative framework to scales and contexts that go well beyond individual relationship scenarios — they build genuine evaluative breadth. Students who engage these directions can assess power and coercion across personal, community, and historical contexts.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific power imbalance and explains how it operates in a relationship
Evaluates the effect on at least one party's autonomy, rights or wellbeing
Proposes a specific action that could be taken when a relationship becomes coercive or disrespectful

nodes.label: Respect and empathy as relational foundations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how respect and empathy actively establish and maintain respectful relationships
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one way in which demonstrating respect or empathy strengthens a relationship; evaluate what this requires from each party
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the rights and ethical responsibilities of individuals in relationships; investigate the characteristics of positive, respectful relationships; propose and evaluate actions that build respect and empathy across different relationship types
wider: Evaluate how public acknowledgement of cultural contributions (e.g. First Nations Australians in sport and community) functions as a form of respect that builds relational trust at community level — not just in individual relationships
Design a scenario-based evaluation tool that assesses whether a relationship demonstrates respect, empathy and equitable power — apply it to at least two different relationship types
Investigate how cultural practices of empathy and respect differ across communities and evaluate what this means for respectful cross-cultural relationships

response_modes.reason: Respect and empathy operate differently across relationship types — peer, romantic, family, online, cross-cultural. Students who only evaluate these in one relationship context develop a narrow understanding that may not transfer. Working across multiple relationship types and cultural contexts builds a more generalisable evaluative capability.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The community-level respect direction (public acknowledgement, cultural contributions) and the cross-cultural empathy direction each reveal that respect and empathy function at scales beyond the interpersonal. Students who engage the wider tier develop an evaluative framework that applies to both individual relationships and community/cultural contexts.
success_criteria: Identifies specific behaviours or practices that demonstrate respect or empathy in a relationship
Evaluates what respect or empathy requires from each party — not just what it looks like from outside
Distinguishes between genuine respect/empathy and performative compliance
